content: Mumps is a contagious disease caused by a virus. Individuals infected with mumps can transmit the virus to others through activities such as coughing, sneezing, or talking. The virus can also spread by sharing items like water bottles or cups, or through close contact such as playing sports, dancing, or kissing. The symptoms of mumps may include fever, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, loss of appetite, and swelling or tenderness of the salivary glands located under the ears or jaw on one or both sides of the face, a condition known as parotitis. Most individuals with mumps recover completely. However, in some cases, mumps can lead to complications, including inflammation of the brain (encephalitis), testicles (orchitis), ovaries (oophoritis), or breasts (mastitis). Additionally, mumps can result in temporary or permanent hearing loss. Mumps remains a common disease in many countries. Travelers who are not vaccinated are at risk of contracting mumps, especially in settings where close contact occurs, such as schools, sports teams, or religious gatherings. The most effective way to protect yourself against mumps is through vaccination. In the United States, the mumps vaccine is routinely administered to children as part of the MMR (measles, mumps, rubella) or MMRV (measles, mumps, rubella, varicella) combination vaccine. The vaccine is given in two doses: the first dose is typically administered at 12 to 15 months of age, and the second dose is given between 4 and 6 years of age. If you were born in or after 1957 and have never had mumps or been vaccinated against it, you should receive two doses of the MMR vaccine before traveling. The second dose should be administered at least 28 days after the first dose. Infants aged 6 to 11 months who are traveling internationally should receive one dose of the MMR vaccine prior to travel, although this dose does not count as part of the routine childhood vaccination series. It is important to note that vaccine protection can sometimes decrease over time. However, individuals who have been vaccinated and still contract mumps typically experience milder symptoms and are less likely to develop complications. Pregnant individuals should not receive the MMR vaccine. Any unvaccinated person should get the MMR vaccine immediately after their pregnancy. Additionally, it is advised to avoid becoming pregnant for at least four weeks after receiving the MMR vaccine.
